THE BUSINESS QUESTION

How can shopping data reveal customer preferences and support more focused marketing and product decisions?

A retail analysis workflow documented through Python preparation, SQL queries and outputs, and a Power BI reporting plan. The report explores purchase amounts, subscriptions, product categories, discounts, reviews, and repeat purchases.

FROM RAW DATA TO INSIGHT

What I worked on.

  1. 01

    Clean the shopping dataset

    Inspected missing values and filled 37 missing review ratings using the median within each product category, preserving category-level differences.

  2. 02

    Engineer useful categories

    Used pandas qcut to create age groups and mapped textual purchase frequencies to days. Removed promo_code_used after identifying redundancy with discount_applied.

  3. 03

    Analyze in PostgreSQL

    Loaded the prepared DataFrame into PostgreSQL through SQLAlchemy. Used aggregations, conditional CASE expressions, common table expressions, and ROW_NUMBER to compare spending and rank products within categories.

  4. 04

    Define the reporting layer

    Outlined Power BI measures for customer count, average review rating, and average purchase amount, with categorical filters for subscriptions, gender, age, and product type.

THE FINDINGS

What the data revealed.

Customers by purchase-history segment

Loyal
3,116
Returning
701
New
83

Counts reproduced from the report’s SQL output, p. 8. Segment labels follow the report’s CASE rules.

A large repeat-customer segment

The report’s purchase-history segmentation counted 3,116 Loyal, 701 Returning, and 83 New customers. These are rule-based groups defined in the SQL.

Similar average spend by subscription

Subscribers averaged 59.49 in purchase amount, compared with 59.87 for non-subscribers. Subscription status alone did not show higher average spending in these outputs.

Age-group contributions differ

Young Adults contributed 62,143 in purchase value, followed by Middle Aged at 59,197, Adults at 55,978, and Seniors at 55,763.

Product-level ranking adds detail

Window functions identified the top three products within each category. Conditional aggregation also compared the proportion of discounted purchases by product.

FROM FINDING TO NEXT STEP

Where the analysis points.

  • Compare customer groups using both average spend and total contribution.
  • Use product rankings and discount patterns to form merchandising hypotheses.
  • Validate proposed loyalty or marketing actions with controlled evaluation before claiming an improvement.

Proposed next steps based on the analysis.

Source & scope

The supplied report contains SQL outputs and Power BI setup guidance, rather than a completed dashboard screenshot. Spending figures retain the source’s unspecified currency units. The findings do not establish the causal effect of subscriptions, discounts, or shipping options.

PROJECT.pdf, pp. 2–9. Customer count is the sum of the reported subscription groups (2,847 + 1,053).
